name: Video Streaming
tagline: Upload, transcode, store in object storage and stream through a CDN
summary: Creators upload a raw file that lands in object storage and a transcode job is queued. Workers produce several bitrate renditions cut into short segments plus an HLS/DASH manifest, also in object storage. Viewers fetch the manifest from a playback API and pull segments through a CDN; the player measures bandwidth and switches renditions mid-stream.

nodes.label: Creator App
nodes.why: Sends a multi-gigabyte file in resumable chunks so a dropped connection does not restart the upload.

nodes.label: Upload API
nodes.role: Accepts uploads, creates the video record
nodes.why: Issues a pre-signed URL so bytes go straight to object storage; the API only tracks metadata and enqueues work.

nodes.label: Raw Uploads (S3)
nodes.why: Cheap, durable and effectively unlimited; the original is kept so renditions can be regenerated when codecs change.

nodes.label: Transcode Queue
nodes.why: Transcoding takes minutes per video; a work queue absorbs upload bursts and lets workers be scaled independently of the API.

nodes.label: Transcode Workers
nodes.why: CPU/GPU-bound and stateless: each job reads the raw file, writes 240p–1080p renditions as 2–6 s segments and a manifest, then acknowledges.

nodes.label: Segments (S3)
nodes.why: Segments are immutable files — the ideal CDN origin. Storage rather than a server serves them so playback scale is not the application's problem.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Titles, owners, visibility, available renditions and processing state need durable, consistent, queryable storage.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: A popular video's metadata is read thousands of times a second; view counts are incremented far more often than they are read.

nodes.label: Playback API
nodes.why: Checks the viewer may watch, records the view and returns the manifest URL (often signed with a short TTL) — the only per-view request that touches the backend.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: The playback API is stateless, so many instances sit behind one address.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.why: Video is almost all bandwidth. Edge nodes near viewers serve the same segment to thousands of players and pull from the origin only on a miss.

nodes.label: Viewer Player
nodes.why: Reads the manifest, downloads segments a few seconds ahead and switches rendition based on measured throughput and buffer level.

flows.name: Upload and transcode
steps: The creator picks a 4 GB file; the app splits it into chunks and asks the API to start an upload.
The upload API creates a video row in 'processing' state and returns pre-signed URLs for each chunk.
Chunks are PUT directly into the raw bucket; the API is told when the last chunk lands and completes the multipart object.
A transcode job {videoId, objectKey} is published to the queue; the API responds to the creator immediately.
A free worker takes the job, streams the original from S3 and runs FFmpeg for each target rendition, cutting 4-second segments.
Segments and the HLS/DASH manifest are written under /videos/{id}/{rendition}/; the writes are idempotent so a retried job overwrites the same keys.
The worker marks the video 'ready' with its rendition list and acknowledges the job; only now does it appear in feeds.

flows.name: Watch with adaptive bitrate
steps: The viewer opens a video; the player asks the backend for permission and a manifest URL.
The load balancer routes the request to any playback API instance.
The API checks visibility and viewer entitlement and signs a manifest URL valid for a few minutes.
Hot metadata comes from Redis (falling back to PostgreSQL on a miss) and the view counter is incremented atomically.

The player fetches the manifest and the first segments from the CDN edge; it starts at a low rendition for fast first frame, then measures throughput and steps up to 1080p, or down when the buffer shrinks.
Only segments the edge has never seen are pulled from S3; a popular video's segments stay cached at the edge and the origin sees a tiny fraction of the traffic.

flows.name: Popular video served entirely from the edge
steps: Thousands of viewers in one region start the same trending video within minutes.
After the first viewer warmed each segment, every subsequent request is a cache hit at the edge — no request reaches storage or the application for the video bytes.

decisions.decision: Pre-transcode every rendition at upload time rather than on demand
decisions.why: Playback must start in under a second at any quality; transcoding on first request would add minutes of latency and make the first viewer pay for everyone. Storage is cheap compared with viewer CPU or waiting.
decisions.tradeoff: Most uploaded videos are rarely watched, so a large share of transcoding CPU and storage is spent on renditions nobody plays. Just-in-time transcoding of cold content or lazy generation of the highest renditions is the usual optimisation once cost matters.

decisions.decision: Object storage as the CDN origin instead of application servers
decisions.why: Segments are immutable, addressable files; S3-style storage serves them durably at any concurrency with no code. The application stays out of the byte-serving path entirely.
decisions.tradeoff: Access control cannot be enforced per request by the app. Private content relies on signed URLs or CDN token authentication, and a leaked URL is valid until it expires.

decisions.decision: A work queue (RabbitMQ) for transcode jobs
decisions.why: Each job is heavy, must be processed exactly once (or idempotently), and needs acknowledgement, retry with backoff and a dead-letter queue for corrupt files — classic work-queue semantics.
decisions.tradeoff: No replay or fan-out to other consumers. If analytics or content moderation also need every upload event, a Kafka topic alongside (or instead) is the better fit.

decisions.decision: Redis in front of PostgreSQL for metadata and counters
decisions.why: A trending video generates far more metadata reads and view increments than the database should absorb; Redis handles both with sub-millisecond atomic operations.
decisions.tradeoff: View counts flushed to the database periodically are eventually consistent and can be lost on a Redis restart without persistence; acceptable for a counter, not for entitlements.

versions.title: Single server, single file
versions.summary: One server accepts uploads onto its disk, stores metadata and serves the original file with HTTP range requests. Works for a handful of users; there is no quality switching and one server's bandwidth is the ceiling.

versions.title: Object storage + CDN
versions.summary: Files move to object storage and are served through a CDN. Bandwidth is no longer the application's problem, but every viewer still downloads the same single-quality file.

versions.title: Async transcoding
versions.summary: Uploads enqueue a job; workers produce multiple renditions and segments so players can adapt bitrate. Uploads become fast and processing scales independently.

versions.title: Playback API and hot cache
versions.summary: A dedicated playback API behind a load balancer handles entitlement, signed URLs and view counting, with Redis absorbing the read and counter load of popular videos.

textAlternative: On the left, a creator app uploads to an upload API, which writes the original into a raw S3 bucket, records the video in PostgreSQL and places a job on a transcode queue. Transcode workers in the middle read the original, write renditions, segments and manifests into a second S3 bucket and mark the video ready. On the right, a viewer's player calls a playback API through a load balancer; the API reads hot metadata and view counters from Redis, falling back to PostgreSQL, and returns a signed manifest URL. The player then fetches the manifest and video segments from a CDN at the top right, which pulls from segment storage only on a cache miss.
